summary_html: A **state agency fails** to meet federal child-welfare performance standards, triggering **funding penalties** or corrective action under the CFSR or Single Audit Act.
authority_html:
- **Child & Family Services Reviews (45 CFR Part 1355)** — performance oversight and penalties  
- **Single Audit Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 7501–7507)** — audit of federally funded programs  
- **Inspector General Act (5 U.S.C. App.)** — oversight authority for HHS/OIG

primary_citations.citation_text: Louisiana - Children’s Code Article 601 et seq. (Children’s Code – Child in Need of Care, includes reporting duties)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the reasonable-efforts requirement of 42 U.S.C. section 671(a)(15) confers no privately enforceable right under section 1983 and creates no implied private cause of action, leaving enforcement to the Secretary's funding-review machinery.
key_cases.relevance: Is the controlling answer to whether a state's federal compliance failure can be litigated by the affected children.
key_cases.quote: the "reasonable efforts" language does not unambiguously confer an enforceable right upon the Act's beneficiaries

key_cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court affirmed reversal of a termination judgment, holding that where reunification is the permanent plan the department must make reasonable efforts to help the parent remove the impediments to reunification - here to obtain suitable and affordable housing - before seeking termination under La. Ch.C. art. 1015(5).
key_cases.relevance: Ties the state's reasonable-efforts obligation to the federal Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act framework.
key_cases.quote: the duty to make reasonable efforts to remove the impediments to reunification does not necessarily stop once the children are removed from the parent's custody

key_cases.case_name: Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that section 1983 is presumptively available to enforce individual rights unambiguously conferred by Spending Clause legislation unless the statute's own remedial scheme forecloses it, and that the FNHRA provisions at issue create such enforceable rights.
key_cases.relevance: It is the modern framework that must be applied before concluding, on the authority of Suter v. Artist M., that a federal child-welfare requirement is unenforceable by the children it benefits.
key_cases.quote: In that respect, our precedent sets a demanding bar: Statutory provisions must unambiguously confer individual federal rights

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that FERPA's nondisclosure provisions confer no individual rights enforceable under section 1983, and that nothing less than an unambiguously conferred right will support a section 1983 action to enforce a federal spending statute.
key_cases.relevance: It states the rights-creating test that governs whether a state's failure to meet a federal child-welfare standard can be litigated at all by the affected children.
key_cases.quote: We now reject the notion that our cases permit anything short of an unambiguously conferred right to support a cause of action brought under § 1983
